{code:sql}WITH 
  archive AS(
	select
		ucr.id as id,
		ucr.created as created,
		ucr.created_hour as created_hour,
		ucr.decision.decision as decision,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.data.user_id') AS user_id,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.data.order_id') AS order_id,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.data.city_id') AS city_id,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.data.driver_id') AS driver_id,  -- null = no match?
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.query.user.basic_info.created_age_in_days') AS created_age_in_days,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.query.user.order_stats.no_of_client_cancelled_orders') AS no_of_client_cancelled_orders,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.query.user.order_stats.no_of_client_cancelled_long_orders') AS no_of_client_cancelled_long_orders,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.query.user.order_stats.no_of_client_did_not_show_orders') AS no_of_client_did_not_show_orders,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.query.payment.user.successful_payments') AS successful_payments,
		json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT",'$.query.payment.user.successful_cash_payments') AS successful_cash_payments,
		ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY json_extract_scalar(ucr."INPUT", '$.data.user_id') ORDER BY ucr.created_hour DESC) AS rn
	FROM archive_analytical.user_cancel_ride_check AS ucr
	WHERE ucr.created_hour >= DATE_ADD('week', -1, CURRENT_DATE) 
		AND ucr.created >= DATE_ADD('week', -1, CURRENT_DATE) 
)
SELECT
	user_id,
	CONCAT ('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/', CAST(user_id AS varchar)) as user_link,
	CONCAT ('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/calculations/user_cancel_ride_check/', CAST(id AS varchar)) as calc_link,
	no_of_client_cancelled_orders,
	created_age_in_days,
	successful_payments,
	successful_cash_payments
	decision
FROM archive
where cast(city_id as bigint) = 666
and (cast(successful_payments as decimal(10,2)) + cast(successful_cash_payments as decimal(10,2))) < 10
and rn = 1
order by 4 desc
limit 5000{code}

Thanks [~accountid:712020:c190ab8b-4add-4eb3-bd6e-ab39d6c1cd0c] the assessment addresses several important points, but I’m equally wondering about the overall contractual structure (along with its wider implications) and dispatcher licensing. And whether our default approach on Ride Booker API is even applicable here. To elaborate,

* In a typical Ride Booker API use case we would treat the API Partner (aka Bolt Business account customer) - here the likes of Virtua, Venue Butler, Tapbox, etc - the contracting party for the transportation services. And they would be owning the customer relation. Making it a b2b relationship as far as we are concerned. Per [slide 2 here|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wLqd9dzRk6BhpGpRoJqZPxT7CaXm47gBXIu3FEwI7U0/edit?slide=id.g351a3d4d4f6_1_43#slide=id.g351a3d4d4f6_1_43] and as expanded in [this document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1tZYYbhGTC9dcsPU-Ng49SimyaIz9qGRQVvxHzqZJZzw/edit?tab=t.0]. That aligns also with the [FinReg|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1AZ6R3pQcPhwHNTbSdXytaZeG3T1CvIgO0N50WP1DcK4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.518o0uvbiq5k] and Tax narratives. *Question:* does the kiosk setup follow the same flows? If not, what changes are suggested to the default flows and why? E.g. Is the Rider contracting directly with the Driver/Transport Provider? What is our relationship with the Rider? All this is central to liability, consumer rights, as well as for the FinReg/Tax narratives. cc [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba] [~accountid:62615f256cb53d006a6a3fe1] 
* Somewhat dependent on the above but should be assessed whether kiosk operators, as intermediaries enabling public ride bookings, could qualify as dispatchers in regulated jurisdictions. If it’s dispatching to the general public. While the immediate risk would lie with the kiosk operator also Bolt could face accusations of facilitating unlicensed intermediation (even if it disclaims liability). Eventually this would have to be assessed on a per market basis. [~accountid:712020:e27975af-e893-46c8-b231-c567323a57ac] but it’s strikes as blurred for me with kiosks. After all, isn’t the expertise of Tapbox and similar providers brining to the market touch screens, not operating in the passenger transportation space in any way(?) _High-level it would make perhaps more sense to me if we treated these third parties as suppliers/ tech enablers to begin with. And as far as the Riders are concerned it’s Bolt with whom they interact, not Tapbox, etc. Bolt owns the customer relationship._ +_In which case however the default Ride Booker API integration agreement should be reviewed accordingly._+

To me these structural questions should be cleared before scaling with kiosks. cc [~accountid:6012ba328fb6ea014a8294ce] [~accountid:712020:70d80a66-553d-4db2-b50f-6bdb7d3bd7a1]

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Issue identified with riders who are blocked due to unpaid rides.
** From 2017-2024, when rider is blocked due to unpaid ride, the rider app states the following to the driver when they open the app: "_Pending payment of #3700 for trip 2017-05-31 16:54:51_ +*_contact Driver +2348060106885_*+". Over 3000 users see this - see [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1RtP3r0ldGZfjpKdmlw1Bl9bo0hrKtM8zrX2kLUN83LI/edit?gid=0#gid=0]. We should not be sharing the driver’s private phone number with the passenger.
** Tickets were created last year, but only assigned to me this year as a low priority. Flagged that this could be picked up in Q3.
* Proposal to fix this is as follows:
** (1) Replace the block message.
*** Privacy to reach out to [#dev-user-auth-support|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06R63EQ6CS] to replace the blocking message by removing driver's phone number for all past and scheduled blockings for all blocked riders. New message should read as follows: "_Please contact Bolt Customer Support team regarding the pending payment of #3700 for trip 2017-05-31 16:54:51_".
*** CS confirmed on Slack that these are custom messages (types by agents), and there are currently no guidelines on this (but CS can add this info). Tat advised this should be included in KB (Michaela Pettersson was responsible).
** (2) CS process for resolving pending payment issues.
*** CS needs to define what their actions should be when they receive a ticket from a user and want to unblock the account.
*** CS previously asked on Slack. CS advised that their current process was to not unblock, but rather the rider should wait for the block to expire (if 3rd report, block is permanent). CS advised we weren’t previously handling the payments as it was not linked to Bolt Balance (i.e., no way of manually getting money to the drivers) - this could be a long term solution. Tat asked that Q4 2024 time was dedicated to resolving the process (Joanna Zylka was responsible).
** (3) Defining status of blocked accounts due to unpaid rides.
*** Some blocks are for 7 years and counting. We cannot justify retaining the rider’s data in a frozen state for so long - we need to either unblock the rider or delete the account. Finance and Legal should decide this.
*** Central Legal already asked on Slack.
* Slack Channel is here: [Link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07J7A924D8/p1724402145651789]

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Ask Michaela if the message was updated.
* Ask Joanna if any updates were made to the process.
* Reiterate Tat’s initial Qs to Merve.

{noformat}SELECT 
		oc.calculation_date,
		oc.calculation_id,
		CONCAT('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/calculations/driver_overcharge_check/', CAST(oc.calculation_id AS varchar)) AS link_to_overcharge_calculation, 
		CONCAT (CONCAT (CONCAT ('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/', CAST(oc.order_token_id AS varchar)), '/' ),CAST(oc.city_id AS varchar)) AS orderlink,
		oc.order_token_id,
		oc.country,
		oc.city_id,
		oc.user_id,
		oc.decision,
		oc.rule_name_array,
		oc.payment_method,
		round(oc.actual_duration_in_min*1.000/oc.predicted_duration_in_min ,3) AS duration_completetion_ratio,
		round(oc.actual_distance_in_meters*1.000/oc.predicted_distance_in_meters ,3) AS distance_completition_ratio,
		round((oc.actual_distance_in_meters + oc.arrived_to_driving_distance) *1.000/oc.predicted_distance_in_meters ,3) AS fallback_bad_status_distance,
		oc.prediction_price_local,
		oc.actual_price_local,
		oc.prediction_price_eur,
		oc.actual_price_eur,
		co.user_price_eur,
		co.partner_price_eur,
		COALESCE(co.refund_amount/co.eur_currency_rate,0) AS refund_eur,
		oc.predicted_duration_in_min,
		oc.predicted_distance_in_meters,
		oc.actual_duration_in_min,
		oc.actual_distance_in_meters,
--		oc.actual_time_to_client_in_min,
--		oc.predicted_time_to_client_in_min,
		oc.accepted_to_arrived_distance,
		round(oc.actual_distance_in_meters/oc.actual_duration_in_min) AS avg_speed_meters_per_min,
		(oc.actual_distance_in_meters / 1000.0) / (oc.actual_duration_in_min / 60.0) AS avg_speed_kmh
--		oc.arrived_to_driving_distance,
--		oc.driving_to_destination_distance_meters,

*_As discussed on Slack on 05.09.2025_* 

h4. {color:#006644}+*Following up on the breach of the confidentiality ring*+{color}

 The written assurances provided have now been reviewed. In summary:

* Caroline Hardey (Lime’s Legal Director) confirmed by witness statement that she did not access the email and has since deleted it.
* Lime’s IT confirmed the email no longer exists in her inbox (though remains in Google Vault, which cannot be deleted without wider data risks).
* Lime’s risk team are aware and will flag any future Vault access requests.

*We considered Bolt’s options:*

* *Injunction:* prospects of success are low, given Lime has already provided assurances via a witness statement.
* *Further written assurances:* unlikely to add meaningful value, particularly as a Lime employee (Alessio Raccagna, Senior Director, Government Affairs - Southern Europe) already sits within the confidentiality ring, and sensitivities exist with ex-Bolt staff at Lime. Liverpool’s Head of Legal also noted a court application would likely carry little merit as no loss to Bolt has arisen.

*That said, we don’t think we should simply let this pass. Our view is that we should:*

# Report the Freshfields solicitor to the Solicitors Regulation Authority (given the breach of duties).
# Rely on the Confidentiality Ring Order undertaking and our correspondence with Liverpool to keep a record of the breach.
# Use this strategically in future tenders, particularly where Bolt is bidding against Lime.

Happy to discuss further if helpful.

Hi! Thanks for tagging me! My comments below:

“_We understand that it can feel frustrating when fares are not recalculated as often as expected. The system is designed to maintain consistency, which means recalculations are rare, even when a shorter route is taken. While this helps keep pricing fair for all, we recognize that it may sometimes feel discouraging. Your feedback is important as we continue to monitor and improve this process_.” - *I think we should reconsider this answer. We should rather say that both the interests of customers and drivers are taken into account and the intention is to make both parties happy. Otherwise, we risk that passengers will no longer consider these services sustainable, which means a decrease in usage. BUT, of course, any feedback from partners is taken into account and analysed in the context of potential changes.*

“_Please know that branded drivers are prioritized in the support system, with Gold and Platinum status tickets placed in the priority queue for faster resolution_.” - *I’m afraid this will lead to discussions about how dependent we make drivers: if the driver doesn’t want to be branded (because he may not want to be exposed), he gets less support from us. Everyone should receive equal treatment when it comes to chatting with the platform. If we are actually making this “selection”, it would be ideal not to trumpet it or to put it in writing in answers that can be shared anywhere.*

“_At the same time, we want to reassure you that branded cars will still have access to the_ *_Travel category_*_, receive_ *_improved exclusive bonuses_*_, and benefit from_ *_status perks_*_. Newly branded cars will be upgraded to_ *_Diamond status_*_, while existing branded drivers will continue to enjoy an average score between_ *_Gold and Platinum_* _each month_.” - *This should not be reminded in a written response. These benefits are on the verge of acceptance anyway, because they can lead to reclassification. They should not be communicated in writing. I am pretty sure that we write it in communications with partners, but in this context, where the driver complains about these problems, such arguments should be avoided.*

Sorina

h3. {color:#4c9aff}+*Meeting Note: London Bikes Weekly Call*+{color}

*Time:* 9:30–10:00am
*Attendees:* Legal, Ops, Public Policy, PR, Product

*Operational Updates*

* *Backlog of repairs:* 430 bikes.
* *Upcoming deployments:*
** *Lambeth:* permit for 575 bikes (v2 of agreement reviewed waiting to receive an update from Lambeth)
** *Westminster:* discussions for 300 bikes (no agreement received yet, waiting for an update).
** *Kensington:* agreement for 600 bikes, but operationally doesn’t make sense if Westminster remains unresolved.
* *New bikes:* 650 arriving in October (off-season). John suggested storing these for a few months.

*Competitor Activity (Lime)*

* Lime redeploys at night, often over capacity.
* They move Bolt bikes out of bays.
* Deployment issues:
** Bolt has 400 deployed; 171 bikes have had no orders in 3+ days.
** RPV < 0.2; users often abandon rides when leaving boroughs, forcing rebalancing.
** 170 rebalances in September (vs. 975 trips in August).
* *User feedback:* Negative experience without access to Westminster (important for trips into Hyde Park & Soho).
* Lime tactics: drop bikes en masse (esp. backstreets, not main high streets).
* *Capacity issue:* Each bay holds 11 bikes. Allocation should be ~2.5 bikes per operator, but Lime places ~11.
* Potential: Increase utilization if capacity caps lifted - but this requires access to more boroughs.
* Ops considering monitoring Lime’s activity

*Expansion Opportunities*

* *Lewisham:* contingent on opening Greenwich first.
* *Greenwich:* prerequisite for Lewisham.
* *Wandsworth:* non-responsive.
* *Islington:* possible window in March 2026.
* *Tower Hamlets:* non-responsive; strategic as Lime & Voi operate there without permits.
* *City of London:* currently refusing to take new operators (capacity issues).

*Warehouse Planning*

* Decision needed by {color:#ff5630}*December 2025*{color}{color:#ff5630} {color}for new warehouse (target May next year).

*December Expectations*

* Management target: *5,000 bikes in London by year-end*.
* *Realistic traget:*
** With Kensington & Chelsea, (and if we signed an MoU with Lambeth, and Westminster) maximum fleet size ~1,500 (based on borough caps).
** 5,000 target is unachievable without new MoUs and further borough agreements which is likely to happen by EOY.

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,
*Billing Ops AI*

[~accountid:712020:70d80a66-553d-4db2-b50f-6bdb7d3bd7a1] if we invoice Tapbox, collect payment from Tapbox and contract with Tapbox reflecting them as the recipient of transportation services then that is aligned with the standard Ride Booker API (b2b) setup. It would be Tapbox owning the customer relationship with the passenger (a third party beneficiary as far as we are concerned). The SMS (with URL) we send to the passenger including ride data and T&Cs can almost be seen as courtesy on our behalf. _Let’s be mindful we shouldn’t be sending the passenger the Rides Customer T&C (as the passenger is not our Customer), but rather the Ride Booker Passenger T&Cs (the first draft version attached_ [_here_|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QZgF13tvigY4U8GNKRnvlaPMn5tjP6NWWQn_WhJVm7k/edit?tab=t.0]_, I should be able to share an improved version for your review by end of this week)._

To further foster that narrative it would ideally be Tapbox owning also the relationship with the airport etc. Appreciate commercially it might make sense for us to have a direct relation here. 

That said, I do have some doubts whether the whole kiosk use case can stand the “duck test” - we have a consumer interacting directly with Bolt branded interface requesting rides over Bolt platform. And assisted - if requested - by Bolt appointed assistants? Moreover should they pay directly at the kiosk as well and receive a payment document for the ride [which I understand is not the case though]. If it looks like a duck, swims like a duck, and quacks like a duck, then it probably is a duck. Closest parallel for me seems to be [Bolt Dispatch|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRODWIKI/pages/3705104851/Bolt+Dispatch] (live for years in AZ afaik) where Rides Ops equally leverages on Ride Booker on the backend but controls the front (in compliance with local laws I assume).

Overall, it’s just smth I would assess against local regulations [~accountid:712020:e27975af-e893-46c8-b231-c567323a57ac] to ensure we’re fine with the likes of Tapbox reselling rides. There might be room to expand on the central assessment as well, cc [~accountid:712020:c190ab8b-4add-4eb3-bd6e-ab39d6c1cd0c] 

Appreciate this current approach might be within our risk appetite while we trial.

Hi [~accountid:712020:58fb140c-5d84-43ea-a489-5c7315d1e8b6] - in my eyes, we don’t need to obtain prior authorisation for the following reasons:

# We aren’t transferring data to an (in)adequate country. 
# We obtain consent to process special personal information, specifically biometric data.

The adequacy mechanism under POPIA is one where the Responsible Party makes its own determination as to the adequacy of a third country, in line with the standards set out under s72. We achieve adequacy through a binding agreement, and the laws and regulations of the recipient country are sufficiently strong either way.

Hope that’s helpful.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Hello,

This is related to a new feature called re-use preauthorisation. Instead of placing a new hold for every trip, we now *re-use an existing pre-authorization* for a set period of time.

This means if you take multiple trips, we use the same hold to cover the cost, so you won't see multiple temporary charges on your statement.

In this specific case, the charge for a new order was simply applied to a pre-authorization from a cancelled order that was already applied on the card.

Cheers,

Afiba
PS! The logic for the G-suite license Okta groups did not use any rules in Okta, it means that a person needed to assign this type of group manually.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Implementation completed. E2E testing incl. Riders and Drivers teams in PRELIVE in progress. Next: bug fixing. A/B Test. Rollout.

*To answer your questions:*

We are correcting an existing issue. Fleet owners were never forced to create satellites, so this best practice was never properly applied.
We’ve done a spot check of the current situation and identified over 1,000 drivers who need to be moved initially. After that, we will periodically check for drivers who have been operating in another city for more than _x_ weeks, and move them as needed. We must allow a certain window of time, because some drivers only work in another city briefly (e.g., a weekend or national holiday) before returning.

----

*Process:*

Example: The Philippine Fleet has 20 drivers in Paris and 10 drivers in Nice. (This could be seasonal or permanent.) Currently, the fleet only has an entity in Paris. This creates two problems:

A. Drivers in Nice are on the wrong commission, which causes issues with our revenue and minimum guarantee compliance.
B. City-level performance data becomes inaccurate.

The process is as follows:

# We check whether those drivers have been operating in Nice for more than _x_ weeks (appropriate window still to be confirmed).
# If yes, we create a Nice satellite (no impact on the fleet owner).
# We move those 10 drivers to the Nice satellite, which fixes data accuracy and applies the correct commission—ensuring minimum guarantees are calculated properly.
# We review and apply the same process this for all fleets on a regular basis.

----

*Long-term:*

This issue applies to both fleets and independents (to a lesser extent). I am working with central ops on a change to how commission is applied. For example, the system could automatically apply the local commission to a driver based on the city where they are currently active. This development requires a major backend billing shift and will take time.

----

*Ideal compromise (if legally possible):*

We send a one-time, generic communication to all fleet owners and drivers stating:

* Starting from [today + 15 days]
* To regularise commission attribution for rides
* And for legal and safety reasons (e.g., knowing a driver’s city in case of an incident—this can be framed positively)
* We will apply the local commission to every driver consistently operating in a given city.
* All driver history and tax information will remain available upon request.

_Optional:_ We could add that in many cases this will result in a favorable commission change. However, this may imply that some drivers are currently paying too much commission, which could be sensitive.



----

*Benefits:*

* By avoiding specific details (satellites, moving drivers, etc.), we retain flexibility to adapt the process in the future.
* When the long-term fix is ready, we will already have communicated the principle, so we’re covered.
* By issuing one generic communication with an execution date of today + 15 days, we cover both the immediate large-scale moves and future cases—without needing to communicate repeatedly.
* Operationally, one big initial communication is far simpler.

# *_What was the goal of the project?_*
## *Here were the project goals:*
##* Providing personalised, proactive learning support to improve confidence and competence.
##* Leveraging real-time data to track progress and identify knowledge gaps.
##* Reinforcing key learning areas to improve retention and training effectiveness.
##* Ensuring agents stay updated on process changes and adapt quickly.
##* Closing knowledge gaps faster to boost overall agent performance.
##* Data goals:
##**  *Improve Quality Scores*
o Customer critical: 90%
o Business critical: 95%
o Compliance critical: 99.5%
##*** *Improve Average Handling Time*
##** o Average AHT: 6mins
## *_What actually happened?_*
##* The 4/5 goals from above were achieved, as the tool itself is ensuring those goals. Content was personalised to the extent it could be, as the tool repeats questions that were answered incorrectly. OS Transcom trainer Viktorija Pultinevičienė confirmed that what agents answered wrongly, those topics were also confirmed as knowledge gaps in the Quality reviews. The retention was improved, as agents had better results over time for the same topics. Knowledge gaps were also identified and closed faster.

The goal “Ensuring agents stay updated on process changes and adapt quickly“ was not reached, as the tool does not serve well for the process change. We changed the questions mid-project to focus more on quality and to have more lasting questions that are not prone to change when the processes change.

##* When it comes to data, we had the following goals in mind, we received 90-day report from the EDF team:
##** QA mean has improved from 89.3 (Sep 24 – Feb 25) to 92.5 (March – June 25).
##** QA for Business Critical has improved from 88.7 (Sep 24 – Feb 25) to 91.4 (March – June 25).
##** QA for Customer Critical has improved from 83.2 (Sep 24 – Feb 25) to 90.6 (March – June 25) - a huge 8.9% improvement
##** QA for Compliance Critical has improved from 98.8 (Sep 24 – Feb 25) to 98.9 (March – June 25)
##** AHT has improved from 8.17 minutes (Sep 24 – Feb 25) to 8 minutes (March – June 25).
##**  The overall average engagement score was 81% and we had only 1 non-engager during first 90 days
##** The overall average competency was 59% during first 90 days


## *_Were we accurate in predicting efforts?_*
##* We were mostly accurate; however, the main issue is that we cannot confidently attribute the improvement solely to Clever Nelly.
##* When Jahanzeb Ahmed Quraishy and Anastasia Pjatakova joined after CS re-org to decide on the next steps of the project, main argument was the above, with an add-on that we signed different contracts with BPOs at the  beginning of the year, which also influenced the quality improvement.



# *_What went well? (Pros)_*
## The tool is easy to use and learners only spend 1,2 minutes on it daily.
## Questions are sent daily automatically in a random manner - no tool we have currently is able to do that.
## The AI targets knowledge gaps, meaning each agent gets a personalised experience based on their needs.
## Reporting and all of the background work are provided by EDF.
## EDF provides access to the dashboards where performance can be monitored daily by us and by the BPOs.
## Reporting offers individual progress tracking, which is useful for TLs.
## The tool allows setting up multiple groups and targeting them with specific questions only - this could be beneficial in a regional setup.
## We saw the improvement in data.



# *_What didn’t go well? (Cons)_*
## The con is mainly the cost.
## The tool is not easily adjustable for constant changes; however, it is not really what the tool is about anyway.
## We cannot directly edit the questions in the tool; we use a sheet template, and we need to send that sheet to EDF every time we make a change.
## We don't track individual performance at this stage in CS. If we were - this would be a great tool, but until we have a clear plan on how to get to the individual performance tracking & get the direct benefits from the tool, we don't have a clear way of measuring its impact. It is not actionable enough to justify the costs.
## We had a big turnover with the agents. Every week, some agents left Transcom (or Bolt project), so new agents were added to the Clever Nelly. This did not ensure consistency in the data.
## Due to the changes and people being let go in the former Knowledge Managemenet team and CS in general, the project had blockers quite a few times and was delayed. Miroslava and Irena took over the project after other people from the KM team were let go, which delayed the start of the project. 
# *_How to avoid this the next time?_*
# *_What else can be improved?_*

co.created,

CONCAT (CONCAT (CONCAT ('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/', CAST(co.order_id AS varchar)), '/' ),CAST(co.city_id AS varchar)) AS orderlink,
co.payment_method_type,

co.user_price,
round(c.sum_tolls*1.00/co.partner_price,1) AS ratio_toll,
c.*
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
JOIN (
			SELECT 
			pf.order_id, pf.city_id,fp."type", fp.final_id, array_agg(fp.name), count(fp.id) AS count_tolls, sum(fp.price) AS sum_tolls
			FROM ng_public.pricing_order_final_price_components fp

			AND fp.created_date >= DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date)
			GROUP BY 1,2,3,4
	) AS c ON c.order_id = co.order_id AND c.city_id = co.city_id  
WHERE
co.country_code = 'ke'

co.created_date >= DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date)

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancel it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/2071227695/307?orderTryId=2553971333|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/2071227695/307?orderTryId=2553971333] and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineers are currently working on sending the right refund amount for these cases where a partial refund was previously made automatically. 
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance to compensate for the debt in their account?

h2. Update

* Dead tasks in profiler related to Shared preferences is a valid behaviour. Shared preferences create threads internally.
* *Migration to coroutines* A significant source of delays are switches between Rx/coroutines, as for some cases app makes multiple conversions like rx → coroutines → rx again → coroutines again, which causes extra thread creation and affects performance. Example:
** Replacing {{UpdateAppStateUseCase}} (Rx) by {{UpdateAppStateSuspendingUseCase}} increases the startup time to 20%
** {{UpdateAppStateSuspendingUseCase}} calls Rx functions with {{await}}. When migrating some of them to Flow/coroutines, startup time reduces back to normal
* *DataStore.* As we often store heavy objects in SharedPreferences and often access them synchronously in startup, we can consider [migration to DataStore|https://developer.android.com/topic/libraries/architecture/datastore]

h2. Follow-up

* Identify the Rx-based logic that is called on startup and make the tickets to migrate these to coroutines
* Identify the SharedPreferences called on startup and try using DataStore there

Bolt Ghana is legally required to participate in the survey. According to Section 25 of the Ghana Statistical Service Act, 2019 (Act 1003), the Government Statistician is authorized to request information, estimates, or returns from individuals and entities on various topics, including transportation, capital formation, commercial and professional undertakings, as well as income, earnings, profits, and interest.

Failure to provide the requested information, estimates, or returns is considered an offense and can result in fines or imprisonment. The Act ensures that all collected data remains strictly confidential, used solely for statistical purposes, and will not be disclosed in a manner that identifies any individual or entity.

Although compliance with the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) surveys is mandatory, Bolt can request details about the privacy safeguards in place for the collected information and opt to submit the data in a protected format (written format within a protected document).

{code:sql}SELECT
month(x.created) AS MONTH,
APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
APPROX_DISTINCT(x.session_id,0.0041) AS count_sessions,
APPROX_DISTINCT(x.user_id,0.0041) AS count_users,
ROUND(SUM(x.max_predicted_price_eur),2) AS sum_predicted_price_eur
FROM (
WITH pred AS (
SELECT 
a.order_id,
a.city_id,
MAX(a.predicted_price) AS max_predicted_price
FROM ng_public.pricing_order_prediction a 
WHERE a.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30' 	
GROUP BY 1,2
)
SELECT 
co.created,
co.id,
conv.session_id,
co.user_id,
p.max_predicted_price*1.00/rate.rate AS max_predicted_price_eur
FROM ng_public.company_order co
JOIN ng_public.etl_fraud_rh_decision_conversion conv ON conv.search_token_id = co.search_token AND conv.city_id = co.city_id AND conv.user_id = co.user_id 
JOIN ng_balance_user.balance_user_billing_transaction bubt ON co.search_token = bubt.source_id AND co.city_id = bubt.source_city_id AND (co.user_id = bubt.target_account_id OR co.user_id = bubt.source_user_id)
JOIN ng_balance_user.balance_user_booking bub ON bubt.id = bub.transaction_id
JOIN archive_analytical.user_order_request i ON i.meta.order_id = co.search_token AND i.meta.city_id = co.city_id 
LEFT JOIN pred p ON p.order_id = co.id AND p.city_id = co.city_id  
LEFT JOIN ng_public.vw_currency_exchange_rates rate ON DATE(rate.valid_on) = DATE(co.created) AND rate.currency = bub.currency
WHERE co.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND conv.order_request_created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND bubt.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND bub.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND conv.order_happened = FALSE 
AND i.created_hour BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND i.decision.pre_auth.amount.value = 0
GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5
) AS x
GROUP BY 1 
ORDER BY 1 DESC{code}

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,

h1. Problem Statement: AWS Account Management & Governance

h2. Background

Our organization is experiencing rapid growth in the number of AWS accounts. At present, we manage approximately *40 AWS accounts*, with new accounts being created on a regular basis. Accounts are provisioned using {{_bootstrap_accounts}} and Terraform, but as the environment expands, this approach is becoming increasingly difficult to scale and govern effectively.

To continue scaling our AWS footprint while maintaining security, compliance, and operational efficiency, we need a more *standardized and automated approach* to account creation and governance.

----

h2. Current Problems

h3. 1. Governance Challenges

* No consistent *naming convention* or account structure (by environment, business unit, or workload).
* Engineers often struggle to quickly identify the *purpose* of an account.
* Lack of a standardized *governance baseline* (e.g., security controls, logging, guardrails).
* Inconsistent application of compliance and security requirements across accounts.
* Limited visibility into *organization-wide compliance posture*.

h3. 2. Operational Overhead

* *Bootstraping a new AWS account is time-consuming* and involves repetitive setup steps.
* Manual work is required to integrate new accounts with central services such as:
** AWS Single Sign-On (SSO) / IAM Identity Center
** Centralized logging (CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Security Hub)
** Budget and cost controls
* High *risk of misconfiguration* due to manual processes and lack of enforced standards.
* Cross-account access and service integration remain *cumbersome* and error-prone.

h3. 3. Scalability Limitations

* Current manual and Terraform-based approach *does not scale* with the pace of new account creation.
* Applying new organizational policies or controls retroactively is difficult.
* Increased risk of *configuration drift* as accounts evolve independently.
* Growing administrative burden slows down engineers and operations teams.

----

h2. Impact

* Slower time-to-value when onboarding new workloads or teams.
* Increased security and compliance risks due to inconsistent controls.
* Higher operational costs and inefficiency in managing accounts.
* Reduced engineer productivity caused by unclear account purpose and setup delays.

----

h2. Opportunity

By adopting *AWS Control Tower*, we can:

* Automate *account provisioning* with consistent guardrails and governance baselines.
* Enforce *organization-wide policies* (naming, tagging, region restrictions, Service Control Policies).
* Integrate accounts seamlessly with central security and logging services.
* Provide a *self-service model* for teams to request accounts without manual overhead.
* Gain visibility into compliance through a *central dashboard*.

This will reduce operational burden, strengthen compliance, and allow us to scale AWS usage with confidence.

Hi Elīna,

Thank you for your detailed guidance and for outlining the key considerations regarding insurance requirements and communication with Fleet Owners (FOs).

I would like to clarify one point regarding the comms: when you refer to communication with FOs, should this be understood as a message that we would need to send out to all new FOs during onboarding, or do you also see a need for a one-time broader communication to all existing FOs on the platform?

Additionally, I wanted to highlight a practical challenge regarding the collection of insurance documentation when FOs are creating these cars in the FOP. In most cases (approximately 90%), the insurance is not yet finalized at the time when the car is created in the system. Typically, it takes up to two weeks for the policy to be issued after the vehicle receives its number plate, although coverage is retroactively valid from that date. Requiring documentation at this early stage may therefore create friction in the process.

In this light, wouldn’t it make more sense to have it specified directly in the T&Cs that it is the FO’s full responsibility to hold all necessary insurances at all times? This way, the obligation is clearly contractual, and the responsibility sits with the FO. If an FO fails to meet this requirement, the liability remains with them.

When combined with the safeguard offered by the insurer, automatic enrollment if coverage lapses or is invalid, this could provide the best of both worlds:

* FOs remain contractually responsible for compliance.
* Bolt avoids operational bottlenecks during onboarding and reduces exposure.
* The insurer provides a safety net to ensure continuous coverage, protecting both sides in practice.

This approach seems to strike the right balance between clarity of responsibility, legal protection for Bolt, and practical efficiency in daily operations.

Hi everyone!

Thank you for all your inputs and thank you [~accountid:5bb1cc64c9dad04734ea835a] for your valuable contribution.

My view on this is that we shouldn’t lean on the Ride Booker B2B narrative for public Bolt-branded kiosks in Malta. It raises intermediary licensing questions for Tapbox.

My advise is to treat vendors as tech suppliers and for Bolt to remain the sole authorised intermediary interfacing with riders. In Malta, if Tapbox owns the rider, takes payment, and the kiosk is public Bolt-branded, TM could argue Tapbox is acting as an intermediary to the public without authorisation — and that Bolt is facilitating that. 

My view on how this should take place, at least in short term (pilot):

* Bolt is the customer-facing intermediary platform (exactly as in the app). The kiosk is just another “web application” entry point to Bolt’s authorised platform.
* Vendors (Tapbox/Venue Butler) are tech suppliers/ processors, not transport intermediaries. They must not present themselves as sellers/resellers of rides or take transport-service risk.
* Merchant of record / payment: Bolt (as commercial agent); avoid vendors taking rider payments for the transport service (that’s what triggers intermediary characterisation).
* T&Cs at kiosk: Show Rider T&Cs. 
* Regulator touchpoint: Send a courtesy note to Transport Malta explaining the pilot UI is an additional booking interface of Bolt’s existing authorised platform; confirm that bookings/logs remain in Bolt’s system in Malta.

*Conclusion:*
Rather than adding a Ride Booker flow, we should treat the kiosk as a straightforward extension of Bolt’s existing platform: an on-site terminal that replicates the in-app experience. This keeps contracting, licensing, and privacy models unchanged and avoids avoidable complexity.

Happy to join an alignment call if useful.

Nevertheless, the appetite of the business is to push ahead with this, and so it will be adopted for the pilot phase (although we may want to reconsider for the feature going forward.
** VK has mentioned on the Malta ticket that the business is open to considering a B2C arrangement / a different template agreement - it is just that B2B has been the only dynamic discussed so far.

+*API Agreement Analysis*+

* Agreement is between Bolt and ‘Partners’ (i.e., those using the Rider Booker API to allow others to order Bolt rides without using the app).
** ‘Demand Partners’ = Corporate customers who use the API to book rides (i.e., Bolt Business Clients ordering rides on behalf of passengers). There is no ‘Demand Partner’ in the case of Tapbox.
* Annex 3 contains data processing terms.
** Processing roles:
*** Bolt and the Demand Partners are independent controllers.
*** Partner is a processor on behalf of the Demand Partner.
*** Annex 3 mentions that if the Partner processes personal data on Bolt’s behalf, the parties will enter into a DPA (2.3). However, processing roles not explicitly identified.
** States that Bolt is sharing full suite of driver information with the Partner.
*** According to Tom, we are sending this to the Partner so that the Partner can show this to the passenger (i.e., showing it in the kiosk).
** Clause 3 requires Bolt to specify in its privacy notice that it shares driver data with Partners and Demand Partners. We can justify this based on updated driver privacy notice, so this is fine.
*** Clause 4.2 requires Bolt to only process user data in line with PN. This creates unnecessary contractual liability, but is ultimately fine.
*** Similarly, Clause 4.3 requires Bolt to not send direct marketing comms to Demand Partners. This is fine, as presumably B2B marketing. Nevertheless, strengthens the argument for switching off marketing comms by default.
** Clause 6 contains a mutual indemnity between Bolt and the Partner.
** Long story short, Annex 3 says the following about Bolt and Partner: (i) they shall share user data between them; (ii) they must comply with data protection laws (Bolt has a few additional obligations); (iii) Partner may be a processor on behalf of Bolt (in which case, DPA is needed); and (iv) international transfer laws must be respected.
* *Conclusion*: 
** Only issues with the Agreement are: (i) the {color:#ff5630}*indemnity*{color}; and (ii) the accuracy of the stated {color:#ff991f}*data sharing*{color} (the former is more important).
** Otherwise, we can separately enter a {color:#ff991f}*DPA/DSA*{color} with the Partner.

Nevertheless, Partner access to API is limited to authorised representatives only, which is good (2.7).|:orange_circle:|Include the usual security provisions in the separate DSA.
Get {color:#4c9aff}*InfoSec to review*{color} the kiosk provider’s suite of security measures, if we cannot get them to agree to ours.|

This is {color:#ff5630}*not enough*{color}.|:orange_circle:|{color:#4c9aff}*Amend the indemnity*{color} to be pro-Bolt (or at least, include regulatory penalties / other losses) +_in future agreements_+. Also, consider carve-out for liability cap.|

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Data Processing Roles - Analysis*
{panel}

* At first glance, my view was that the kiosk provider was a _processor_.
** Given that we design the order flow, Bolt determines what data is to be collected, and it appears that the kiosk provider does not have any say in what data is relayed between Bolt and the passenger (it is effectively mainly an interface).
** Some of the key providers (e.g., TapBox) do not have an obvious privacy notice to make the case that they act as a controller.
** Tom Bishop initially said that Tapbox (in terms of processing) “_should only be doing it on Bolts instructions_” ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C099SBLJ42E/p1761235829532299?thread_ts=1760345585.470629&cid=C099SBLJ42E]) - this suggests a [DPA|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ezFeNGwxwQXdST451Fb_OiDlOaYOJybJ3aMGguNWpF0/edit?tab=t.0] would be better.
** We also want to keep the kiosk provider on a ‘tight leash’ regarding data processing, in case they suffer a data breach. As it is Bolt’s name on the kiosk, the passenger would be more likely to go after Bolt if things went wrong.
* However, ultimately, we have settled on an *_independent controller_* relationship with the kiosk providers 💡 
** At least for the pilot phase, we are adopting the API Integration model. This is a standard Bolt Business setup, and the usual approach here is to characterise the business customer as an independent controller (see [T&Cs|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_Spbzn3CiKfxJDWxKCR1VovWO8C9Yo00mzHr50dBh2U/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.2w1kcq7ofs1m] and [Addendum|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1I4hfO6VtTKDG9necgATHzBUUTE0gTf9kzBNZ4wRyAA8/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.kmrojrdg2vf3]), who is purchasing rides on behalf of passengers. 
*** Originally, this model seemed ill-fitting to us and Legal, and it was flagged that in the long term we might be entering a B2C setup in any event.
*** However, in November 2025, it was confirmed that: (i) the API Integration model is in fact applicable to the setup, with the kiosk provider effctively being a Bolt Business customer; and (ii) the kiosk providers tend to act as independent payment collectors (we then invoice them on a monthly basis) who has a relationship with the passengers. Both of these factors suggest the classic B2B / independent controller setup that we use in an API integration context.
** Certain providers (e.g., TapBox - see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08C50GNLHE/p1764240906322919?thread_ts=1763034470.610829&cid=C08C50GNLHE]) stores trip records in its own logs, and so uses the data for its own purposes. “_This is to be able to provide support, if there are any issues reported_”. This is a key point, and is more indicative of a IC relationship.
** Also, we can argue that the kiosk provider is the one that first collects the passenger data and stores it on its own systems, before sending entering it into Bolt’s systems (via the API Booker) to book a trip.
* We are therefore going for the DSA model for the kiosk setup for now, unless the model / setup later changes.
** For Virtua, we are preparing a ‘global framework’ agreement. This contains our standard DSA ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O7UQJzQAACEujR3XSiGaAr8_vPxC3pGZDh06UhCcmX4/edit?tab=t.0]), which has been adapted from the B2B DSA, as well as a term saying that if a processing relationship is found then the parties will cooperate to prepare a DPA.
** For TapBox, the timetable has accelerated for entering an agreement in certain countries (e.g., LV). We have provided light-touch DSA provisions as an interim measure ([here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zijYm9YNgP-6D10xVBTLGYLfkM76sbhf/edit#heading=h.cgl704cyhk8t]), on the understanding that the global agreement will later be used.

# Liability is capped at *€5 million*.

Hey team, Bolt Drive is working on an initiative to allow users to share their driving score through messages, social media etc. I’ve flagged that this will likely potentialise any negative trends, such as bad PR, GDPR data access requests, data act requests, complaints in general from users, authorities’ scrutiny etc.

I wanted to check with you if there are any additional issues or requirements from the Privacy side we should take into account.Figma visualisation available here: [https://www.figma.com/design/Fub6q52pNtl5t32AmmX7UU/-Drive--Safety?node-id=12738-41422&t=L1WySTdPCqRnbnhE-4|https://www.figma.com/design/Fub6q52pNtl5t32AmmX7UU/-Drive--Safety?node-id=12738-41422&t=L1WySTdPCqRnbnhE-4|smart-link]

Thanks for flagging this, I agree with your raised concerns. Here are additional considerations:

* sharing might trigger additional requests to remove or delete data from external social media or messaging platforms. We would need to clearly outline limitations of Bolt’s responsibility once data is shared externally;
* limiting shared data to strictly necessary details, such as only the numeric driving score or high-level descriptive categories (e.g., "Good," "Great"). Avoid sharing detailed telemetry data (e.g., exact location, speed details, harsh events). The scope of data-sharing must be clearly explained; and
* inform users explicitly that sharing is entirely voluntary.

Overall, users with low scores or users publicly contesting scoring accuracy could lead to significant reputational harm. It would be better if we used only internal channels for complaint resolution to manage this risk proactively.

Hi [~accountid:712020:42b2886c-722b-4c93-b02e-ff673b990b6e] Thank you for raising the ticket!

In Azerbaijan, AR blocking is already available and the market is classified as class 1 from a reclassification perspective. Even though reclassification is not a pressing issue locally, it makes sense to stay aligned with the approach we already use in Europe and Africa. We can therefore use the attached template, where KPIs are measured at the fleet level in aggregate rather than applied to individual couriers. This way, the responsibility and decision-making remain with the fleet, while still giving us a clear basis to monitor and improve performance.

Applying KPIs directly at courier level would increase the perception of Bolt managing individual working conditions. Even if this is not a current issue locally, it could create unnecessary exposure down the line. A safer approach is to link courier bonuses to the fleet’s overall performance: Bolt rewards the fleet, and the fleet then distributes the incentive among its couriers as it sees fit.

Please let me know if there’s anything additional I can support you with!

To close this gap, we should expedite an in-app notification shown before ride confirmation. For now, the simplest approach is a generic disclaimer that some vehicles may be equipped with cameras, which satisfies the bylaw. Later, we can refine this by linking disclosures to driver declarations about whether a camera is installed.

Implementing this now will:

* Give us a defensible compliance position with the City.
* Show regulators we’ve taken proactive remedial steps.
* Reduce reputational risk with riders.

Even a short interim notice would strengthen our position.

Hi [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] 

* *Overall risk - not high, more likely - low-medium depending on the exact approach*
** I wouldn’t call this high risk, since it’s only for Latvia and only for couriers.
** Latvia/Baltics generally not considered high risk for privacy/marketing enforcement.
* *B2B vs B2C*
** Even though this is aimed at couriers, regulators will likely see this as *B2C*, especially at the stage where no the courier does not have a business entity established.
** Our standard approach is to treat drivers/couriers as B2C anyway.
* *If treated as B2C*
** ePD Art. 13(2) applies → “soft opt-in” approach.
** Question is whether a lead’s failed registration attempt counts as a “purchase of products/services.”
** In Latvia, I am not aware of marketing guidelines on this, so the argument could be made - but it’s still a *grey area*.
* *Timing of outreach*
** *Recent rejections (up to ~1 month):* lower risk, complaints/regulator escalation less likely.
** *Old rejections (months/years):* *much higher risk*, people won’t expect contact from Bolt anymore → unbalanced.

Previously with drivers, I advised not to reach out to driver leads who were rejected. Per my information, this is is followed by Driver LCM.

----

Wider note on risks - I remember I flagged this in Slack last year - upon courier registration, couriers are not presented with a privacy-marketing disclaimer (screenshot). I suggested that we include a disclaimer similar to what we have for drivers - [https://bolt.eu/en-ee/driver/|https://bolt.eu/en-ee/driver/|smart-link] . Example of the disclaimer:

{quote}_Following your sign-up, we will occasionally send you offers and promotions related to our services. You can always unsubscribe by changing your communication preferences._{quote}

!Screenshot 2025-09-09 at 16.51.03.png|width=25%,alt="Screenshot 2025-09-09 at 16.51.03.png"!

This is important for ePD Art. 13 compliance - without it, we have a weaker position defending our reliance on soft opt-in approach to couriers globally.

Thanks [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] for the clarifications 🙂 Fully understood that the _Demand_ Partner is not a processor for Bolt. However, I would note the following regarding the _Partner_:

* Annex 3 of the Agreement specifies the processing relationship between: (i) the Demand Partner and Bolt; and (ii) the Demand Partner and the Partner. However, it does not explicitly say what the relationship between Bolt and the Partner is - the only indicator we have on this is Clause 2.3, which demands a data _processing_ agreement between Bolt and the Partner if a controller-processor relationship is found.
* Bolt is ultimately deciding on what data to collect and why, whereas the Partner is effectively executing Bolt’s instructions here (except for perhaps minor analytics purposes).
* There are advantages to characterising the Partner as a processor, as it means we have a tighter leash on what the Partner can and cannot do with the data and can implement tight controls (since Bolt is the user-facing entity here, we want to avoid situations where Partner negligence results in passsenger complaints against Bolt)

IMO, all of these factors steer me towards the *_Partner being a processor on behalf of Bolt_*, rather than an independent controller with Bolt - which would suggest that we need a separate Article 28 agreement. In any case, the API Integration Agreement is already signed, so this would probably be the more pragmatic approach.

If you disagree with this approach (or if I have still misunderstood the dynamic here, in which case apologies for being slow!) let me know and we can discuss over Slack 🙂

We have this project on our backlog in safety. Here’s the [RFC|https://docs.google.com/document/d/11ZxXxgCwNnwcsVH_KmGbmN2MJV1xcJ-68B9-MhaQlr4/edit?tab=t.0]. We look at it from an ‘adding CCTV info to driver profile’ perspective first.

If I remember well, we estimated a 4 MWs effort for mobile, and 2MWs effort for back-end. We touch driver and rider app. The notification from rider app should be straight forward. The problem lies on collecting the info first from drivers.

First I’d point the question of Ronald → Was this risk not assessed before launching? and also how we see this going forward. This feature is not in our priorities at least in the next 3 months.

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,
*Billing Ops AI*

Hi!

Regarding campaign material for the new campaign: 

*Concept: Gustav Vasa in 2025*

Instead of Queen Silvia, the main character will be Gustav Vasa (a former Swedish king from the 16th century who is well-known in Sweden). Our idea is that he suddenly appears in the year 2025 and navigates modern-day Stockholm. We would follow him for a full day through a series of humorous scenes.

Here are some potential moments from a video where we could weave in our safety features in an entertaining way:

* Gustav Vasa moves through Stockholm and complains that they've renovated a bit too much.
* Comedic scenes, such as: He tries to pay with old coins and is horrified to discover he is no longer on them, or he walks up to his own statue, takes off his hat, and bows. Someone walks by and places a coin in his hat, and Vasa says: "Ah, tax collection still works. Excellent."
* To integrate the safety features, we can play on his historical paranoia. For example, he could ask Bolt's support if they think the driver is a supporter of Nils Dacke (His biggest enemy). Or, when the "Ride Check" feature activates because his car has been stationary for a while, he becomes very impressed that they are checking to ensure he hasn't been abducted by the Danes.

*Rationale:*

Instead of using a living celebrity, we are using a historical figure who has been dead for 500 years, meaning his personal brand cannot be affected by our campaign. However, we still maintain a high level of recognition and humor, as everyone in Sweden knows who he is. It’s an entertaining way to create content where we can subtly introduce our safety features, avoiding the often dull tone of typical safety campaigns.

Does that provide enough information?

/Robin

Hi Hazel,

Thank you for reply. Let me share a few thoughts from our side.

Removing the event category from the EFR calculation would reduce visibility into case volumes but wouldn’t address the *core issue of private hire drivers appearing in the wrong vehicles.* Since this falls under Compliance, then it is best to raise it with the relevant team to explore potential improvements. It is a matter that can and should be addressed more directly.

Additionally, it’s important to note that this event category plays a key role in the UK safety processes. It was introduced as a mitigation measure to address reclassification risks, and removing it from EFR calculations will mean we will reduce market support.

Also, if the EC is removed from EFR, the data that the Safety agents currently collect through Cognito will lose its value, which could lead to the EC being removed from the Safety scope altogether. However, we still believe this topic clearly falls under user safety, even if the case volume or attention differs by market. In high-risk reclassification markets, it remains a critical part of our safety framework.

Happy to discuss further if needed.

{quote}Dear Jelena,

Thank you for your message. We understand your concerns regarding the presence of a CCTV camera in a vehicle during your ride.

As previously mentioned, it is important to clarify that drivers using the Bolt platform are independent providers and not employees of Bolt. As such, with respect to Bolt’s responsibility as a platform provider, please note that under the GDPR each party is responsible only for the personal data processing it controls. Bolt is the controller for the personal data processed in connection with our platform and services. If a driver installs and uses their own CCTV device, they do so as an independent data controller under data protection law. This means they are solely responsible for ensuring that any such recording complies with the GDPR and national legislation, including providing passengers with adequate notice and identifying a valid legal basis for the processing. Bolt does not provide, install or control these devices, nor do we have any direct access to or use any recordings made through them.

For this reason, we are not in a position to provide you with a privacy notice for CCTV, as this falls under the responsibility of the driver who operates the system. Bolt’s own privacy notice, which governs how we process personal data in connection with our platform, is available here:[https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|smart-link].{color:#ff5630} {color}With respect to compliance, Bolt does not monitor or regulate the use of CCTV systems in drivers’ vehicles, as this is outside the scope of our services. Each driver is independently obliged to ensure that their data processing practices are in line with GDPR and local requirements.

We have forwarded your concerns to the driver’s fleet to make them aware of the issue. Please rest assured that we take reports of potential privacy breaches seriously and always ensure that they reach the responsible party. In addition, should we get contacted by the competent authorities in relation to this matter, we will cooperate fully to support their investigation.

We hope this clarifies the situation and thank you once again for bringing your concerns to our attention. Should you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to contact our customer support team.

Sincerely, 

Bolt{quote}

Thank you,

Afiba

* Yes, we've seen cases where users report that their email is used on Bolt accounts they don't own.
[#dev-user-data-support|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C06RUSHTRA4] has introduced a feature where users in this situation can remove their emails from Bolt accounts.
Looking at the [sent emails to this address|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/comms-email/emails/sent/?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22start_date%22%3A1756799237.893%2C%22end_date%22%3A1757404037.893%2C%22type%22%3A%22all%22%2C%22status%22%3A%22all%22%2C%22search%22%3A%22hana68hana68%40gmail.com%22%7D%7D] there are several of them and they all should have a link in the footer similar to "Not sure why you received this email?" that starts the removal process.
* Are you considering to do this action [NDLR: deleting the account]? If the account has rides history it's probably not advisable. We can instead remove first name, last name and the email address from the account. And the next time this user logs in, the app will ask them to fill back in these details. If Person A goes through the email address removal themselves, Person B will no longer be able to use this email address (please confirm with [#dev-user-data-support|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C06RUSHTRA4] that this is true). However, we can't prevent them from using the same first and last name.
* [NDLR: should this be reported to fraud?]

Huawei devices change IDs frequently and they are not reliable. And I checked the authentication methods tab where a Google account was used - it was added on the Huawei device ({{linked by device}} column) and also used on the Xiaomi device ({{last used by device}} column). So I'd say it's the same person with 2 different physical devices.

After removing duplicate Driver IDs, I ended up with 101 unique drivers.

For benchmarking, I used the UK EFR for the period January 2024 – September 2025, which is *5.453*. Comparing the drivers’ EFRs against this benchmark:

* 26 drivers had at least one safety event logged (all events included, regardless of reported user type).
* 21 of those drivers had a higher EFR than the benchmark.

Across the group, the overall EFR was *7.932*, which is about 46% higher than the UK benchmark for the same time period. There are a few observations though:

* Some drivers recorded no rides at all during the period (or very few rides).

* A couple of drivers stand out as outliers with a high number of events (Driver ID 1370657 with 17 events, Driver ID 4807573 with 11 events).

To give more context, I’ve added both the number of months with available ride data and the average monthly rides for each driver.

I’ve also included the [list of events|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1k6_mzSj9ebe-HxhpQm1KHY1yAuUsdKOb7JQVaO7edz4/edit?gid=0#gid=0] for reference. Since these are mostly Driver events, perhaps it would make sense to instead look at the EFR for Rider events. What do you think?

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancel it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineers are currently working on sending the right refund amount for these cases where a partial refund was previously made automatically. 
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance to compensate for the debt in their account?

Hello, apologies for delay with the response. The issue arising, since Bolt calculates and stores the Ride price in the gross amount initially, and then if Driver is VAT-liable, we calculate the VAT amount and the amount w/o VAT. 

I attached the calculation here: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1MsJuvV0jPJ2agJyGYz1xfEkejQSNfOzSxZi0bM2DL0Q/edit?gid=635709749#gid=635709749|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1MsJuvV0jPJ2agJyGYz1xfEkejQSNfOzSxZi0bM2DL0Q/edit?gid=635709749#gid=635709749|smart-link] 

Indeed, the 1593.30 / 1.23 = 1295.37, which is amount that is different from the one, when all of the Orders are summed. In the column V, I added the true (not rounded value of the VAT per row) by dividing the total amount of each ride by the 1.23. When adding up all of the values there, we receive the exact amount on the invoice.

Mainly why this happens, or why we are contacted, is that the users have deleted their previous accounts or try different methods to get more promo codes. Not always is this of course visible, and in that case you would be correct in contacting us.

Additionally, if there is only 2-3 people reporting that something is problematic, then most likely it is false. If promo code was problematic, we would have at least 10x the amount of requests.
However, if ever in doubt, please do contact us, better safe than to be sorry.

Hello [~accountid:712020:35a97e3f-8900-4a3a-9057-4ff989d01fe4],
We completed the analysis from our side and found root cause of the issue. 

The aim here was to find those users for whom we trigger 20+ EUR pre-auth amounts. And results showed the issue being related to number of specific card_model_id launched under {{everyday_suv }}category. I have summarised the issue below, what we have done so far and the future steps to prevent this:

*Root Cause*

* Each car category has different backend configurations for pre-authorization thresholds.
* These thresholds depend on:
** Premiality level of the category (premiality ≈ risk level)
** Country-level risk configuration
* For everyday_suv:
** Premiality level is set to “medium” with no exception on the latest card models ids 
** Combined with the country risk configuration, this is yielding high pre-auths for many users.
* The volume spike is concentrated on the newly launched car model ids 

h3. What happened?

* We did not receive any information about such changes from the drive team, would be good to check user portfolio and keep an eye on pre-auth amounts or even risky users. 
* The increase was *gradual*, so it didn’t immediately surface in dashboards

h3. Actions

* We sent the relevant car_model_ids to engineering team, they will make changes for premiality level and set thresholds to low instead of medium for certain model ids for Latvia. 
* Next steps:
** I am currently working on creating task for our team to revisit *premiality thresholds for different countries* (we currently are also doing reviews for other countries where this category is live as well). 
** Align with *local/Drive teams* on thresholds to avoid unnecessary high pre-auths.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt Ops OU wants to enter into a partnership with Fortum (EV charging company in Finland).
** Under partnership, Fortum will give Bolt drivers a discount on EV charging through the Bolt Rewards program.
* Partnership agreement has been prepared (on main ticket). We have been asked to review.
** NB. Effectively similar in setup to [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-53344|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-53344|smart-link]. 

+*ANALYSIS*+

* *Partnership Agreement*: No comments (/) (standard template)
** Between Estonian and Finnish companies.
** Obligations:
*** Bolt provides ‘visibility’ services to the partner (i.e., showcasing the promotion to drivers) on the app / platform.
*** Partners provide benefits / offers to drivers.
** Liability:
*** Partner indemnifies Bolt in connection with any breach of law.
** Data processing relevance:
*** Clause 5 - Bolt can use metrics from the rewards program for analytics purposes.
*** Clause 11 - Parties are independent controllers, and shall comply with their respective obligations. If if the parties intend to share any driver personal data, they should enter into a data sharing agreement (11.3).
*** Appendix 1 links to our standard DSA ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/198wvBxxAqwBh7jOp-Lqx87uTlGtIvvzDY5zw1vksoFc/edit?tab=t.0]).
* *Data Sharing*:
** Felix Antwi has sated “_We will not be sharing any driver level data with the partner. So DSA is not needed_” - I doubt this is true. However, Andreas has confirmed “_Bolt will have to share details to the partner of the drivers that are eligible for the specific rewards at each level, so e.g. phone number/email that the partner can use to map right accounts on their end_”
** A DSA is therefore required per Clause 11.3. This is already linked via Annex 1, but is not yet populated.
*** This is fit for purpose, but non-applicable provisions should be removed and yellow highlight should be populated.
* *Marketing*:
** Take usual approach - As this is third-party marketing, drivers must have consented to direct comms.
* *Other* *Issues*:
** If the driver data is being collected by a form, we should check the driver is not being asked for their consent to data sharing - this is an approach the business loves to take with Bolt Rewards, and creates issues.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Is this the only data that is being shared? We need a comprehensive list of the personal data being shared between these parties (and why).
** Through what mediums are we marketing this to drivers?
** How are we getting this data from drivers? Via their profile or via a form when they sign up for the reward?
* Actions:
** Update the DSA to reflect the reality of data sharing.
** Review any applicable forms.

Thanks [~accountid:712020:6ec9ea6b-f071-41dc-ab0a-54910568f43d] and [~accountid:5d1b218591943f0d2ac52db0] - I have a few questions on this before providing my final advice:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *Data sharing*: Are you able to provide a _full list_ of the categories of driver personal data that will be shared here (together with the direction of the data sharing, and the purpose), rather than just examples?
# *Marketing*: Please provide a _full list_ of the mediums through which Bolt will be presenting this promotion / encouraging Bolt drivers to use Fortum’s discounts (e.g., emails, in-app notifications, texts, a post on the landing page, etc.).
# *Collection of participating driver data*: Before sending data to Fortum, how will we be getting the data from drivers? Will we be taking this from their profiles, or will they be providing it via Bolt via a form? If the latter, please provide a copy of the form so that I can take a look.
{panel}

Subject to the above (+*please confirm first*+), my advice is likely to be as follows:

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
* *Partnership Agreement:*
** No comments from a privacy POV (/)
* *Data Sharing:*
** Per Clause 11.3 of the Partnership Agreement, if any driver personal data is being shared (it sounds like this is the case), we should ensure that we enter into a *Data Sharing Agreement* with Fortum. I see that a template has been linked at Annex 1, but this is not yet completed.
** I have included a draft DSA as Appendix 2 - Please populate the yellow highlighted sections with the details of the counterparty and of the data transfers 🙏
* *Promotional Comms:*
** Where we are using *targeted* means (e.g., emails, push notifications, in-app comms) to encourage Bolt drivers to use Fortum’s services, we should only do so for users that have *consented* to receiving comms about third-party products and services (i.e., those who have consented to ‘Partner Offers’ on their account) (!) 
*** Where we are promoting Fortum’s services to Bolt drivers via *untargeted* means (e.g., banners and webpages, not at specific users / user categories), we *do not* need to obtain the driver’s consent in this way (/) 
** In the comms, we should always provide drivers with the option to *unsubscribe* from them (we are likely doing this already, but just flagging for completeness) (/) 
{panel}

There are couple of aspects we need to discuss before you can proceed live with this category as it does entail a lot of fraud risk.

I’ll simply list our main question points here:

# How we can prevent fraud best in your market in this scenario?
## Pre-authorising/Booking whenever we can the first hour/predicted payment to ensure a working payment method: _does_ _depend on user payment method as well_
## Adding a Capturing logic for payments to avoid high user debt but to keep as much as we can from the pre-booked amounts: _does_ _depend on user payment method and final price difference to what we hold vs what accumulated extra_
# How we can limit fraud?
## Perhaps to limit the category only to trusted users and spenders?
## Perhaps to add a final limit to the possible destinations update (trip length)? Not to allow fully endless driving through destination updates.
# How we can resolve fraud? ← This may be even the most important aspect for our discussions
## Are we covered in the local T&C to potentially protect Bolt? Under which conditions?
## Setting up the monitoring and operational procedure to ‘save’ Bolt and action any intentional fraud scenarios
### The right to deduct ride fare due to fraud from the driver-partner (also before it is paid out)
### The right to limit access to this category for those not ‘qualifying’ due to fraud suspicion
